claims.text: The baseline CoCrFeNi alloy has a relatively coarse-grained, unmodified microstructure.
Severe plastic deformation followed by short-duration annealing will produce a stable nanohierarchical microstructure in CoCrFeNi.
The processed microstructure will contain an ultrafine or nanograined matrix.
Short annealing will form uniformly dispersed, thermally stable nano-precipitates in CoCrFeNi.
The annealing-induced nano-precipitates may be Cr-rich phases.
The nanohierarchical grain-and-precipitate structure will enable adaptive friction-interface protection from room temperature to 800 °C.
At lower temperatures, the ultrafine matrix will accommodate interfacial plastic deformation through its high density of grain boundaries.
Enhanced plastic accommodation by the ultrafine matrix will reduce the coefficient of friction at lower temperatures.
At elevated temperatures, nano-precipitates will promote formation of a dense protective glaze layer.
A dense high-temperature glaze layer will suppress adhesive and oxidative wear.
The glaze layer will minimize direct metal-to-metal contact.
The processed CoCrFeNi alloy will have a significantly lower coefficient of friction than untreated CoCrFeNi throughout 25–800 °C.
The processed CoCrFeNi alloy will have a significantly lower wear rate than untreated CoCrFeNi throughout 25–800 °C.
The coefficient of friction and wear rate of processed CoCrFeNi will be relatively temperature-invariant from room temperature to 800 °C.
Untreated CoCrFeNi generally has higher friction and wear rates, particularly at elevated temperatures.
The proposed performance boundary is sliding in ambient air under 5–10 N from approximately 25 °C to 800 °C.
Long-term nanostructural stability under prolonged high-temperature sliding is uncertain and may depend on annealing and processing parameters.

The hypothesis can be tested by comparing identically loaded and heated treated and untreated CoCrFeNi samples while measuring friction, volume-loss wear rate, grain growth, and precipitate stability.

Failure to obtain more than 50% improvement in both friction coefficient and wear rate over the full temperature range, or observation of accelerated grain or precipitate coarsening, is specified as falsifying evidence.
